summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest count of any Brazilian state in the ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind only Ceará and Minas Gerais at 8 each, against a national total of 80. Valor Internacional independently reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026. The state's annual figures have fallen from 13 in 2022 to 9 in 2023 and 8 in 2024, so 2025 is the lowest count since 2022, but it remains among the highest in the country. Over six years Pernambuco recorded 83 violent deaths of trans people, sixth-most in the national ranking for that period, within a Northeast regional total of 349 killings from 2017 to 2025.

The danger is concentrated away from Recife. Roughly two-thirds of such killings occur in interior municipalities rather than the state capital, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker. On 2 October 2025 a trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive, with no arrests reported at publication. On 7 July 2021 Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe, also in the Agreste, killed by several knife strikes; Pernambuco's Civil Police told press that a 22-year-old suspect known as 'Gaúcho' was lynched by locals at the scene. Both cases fall outside the Recife capital region.

Pernambuco stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and after the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes. Courts have also applied the anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed in Pernambuco as elsewhere in Brazil. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. National norms also give LGBTQ prisoners the right to a special, separate place in Brazilian prisons, to be addressed by their social name rather than birth name, to be forwarded to women's prisons by gender identity, and to choose male or female clothing; same-sex partners have had the right to conjugal visitations in all Brazilian jails since February 2015 under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine, documenting housing in masculine-operated units and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of Brazil and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.
tangentialFactors:
Pernambuco's interior municipalities, where roughly two-thirds of trans killings occur, are also where monitoring and access to public policy are weakest, so a visitor spending time outside Recife faces a documented gap in protection machinery rather than only a higher raw count.

The national pattern of violence against trans people persists across cycles: 122 trans people killed in Brazil in 2024 per ANTRA, 80 in 2025, with death threats and intimidation directed at nearly 1,000 transgender candidates in the October 2024 municipal elections even as trans officeholders tripled.

Drink-spiking robberies targeting LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo nightlife, documented in a May 2024 investigation, indicate that nightlife risk to trans visitors is not confined to Pernambuco and is not limited to lethal violence.

outOfScopeNotes:
